summary_md: Snowberg, Wolfers and Zitzewitz (IZA DP 1996, 2006; later QJE 2007) estimate how U.S. presidential outcomes move asset prices. Their key move is identification: on election nights 2004 and 2000, shocks to the market probability of a Bush win (a faulty afternoon exit poll that cut his odds from about 55 to 30 percent and then reversed; the Florida calls in 2000) are treated as exogenous, and asset changes are divided by probability changes (Wald ratios). In 2004 a Bush win raised S&P futures about 1.5-2 percent (0.016 at 10-minute differences, n=104), 10-year yields 11-12 basis points and December 2004 oil about 1.07 dollars. Over 1880-2004 a market-based partisan surprise (Republican indicator minus pre-election probability) implies 2-3 percent higher equities under a Republican president. The methodological lesson matters most for Paul: a daily campaign-period regression of prices on win probabilities gave equity coefficients about ten times the election-night estimate and flipped the oil sign, because the economy moves the odds (reverse causation) and common news moves both. OLS is only an upper bound if political and economic shocks correlate non-negatively. For Mentat this bears on the sector growth study: SEATS-W regresses weekly Democratic giving share on prior-week changes in 538 expected seats (2022 House, -3.47 pp per seat, one election, EXPLORATORY), and SHIFT uses expected-minus-current control. Lagging the forecast fixes ordering but not common shocks, so SEATS-W is a correlation, not a donor response. The paper also suggests a sharper design: event windows around discrete forecast jumps and a surprise-coded shock. It says nothing about networks, lobbying or ranks.

bearings.paper_claim: Daily campaign-period regressions of S&P on Bush re-election probability (June 2003-Oct 2004) give 0.087 daily, 0.128 five-day, 0.243 twenty-day, about ten times the election-night 0.016-0.020; oil coefficients flip sign (-7.27 five-day, -12.57 twenty-day vs +1.07 intraday). Authors attribute this to reverse causation and third-factor shocks; OLS is an upper bound only if shocks correlate non-negatively.
bearings.paper_location: Campaign-period section, Table 2, p.9-12 and fn 14; discussion p.19-20
bearings.system_side: SEATS-W regresses the weekly Democratic share of giving on the prior week's change in 538 Lite expected Democratic seats, pairing each week with the latest forecast available strictly before it starts; 2022 House result -3.47 pp per seat (17 weeks, block-bootstrap p .0086/.0174, Holm .034/.070), one election, EXPLORATORY. The component assumes as-of forecasts precede spending.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Transfers as a design caution: the as-of lag removes reverse ordering within a week but not common shocks (a national news event that moves both forecasts and donor behaviour, or giving that funds campaigns that then move polls). The paper shows such confounding can inflate magnitudes tenfold and reverse signs, so the negative SEATS-W slope cannot be read as donors moving toward or away from the expected winner. Asset prices differ from PAC giving (lumpy, deadline-driven), so the size of the bias does not transfer, only its existence.

bearings.paper_claim: Identification from discrete, plausibly exogenous jumps in win probability (exit-poll leak moving Bush odds 55 to 30 to 95 percent; Florida calls in 2000) with Wald ratios (asset change over probability change), plus split-sample checks for within-window reverse causation (fn 9).
bearings.paper_location: p.4-9, Figures 1-3, Table 1, fn 7 and fn 9
bearings.system_side: SEATS-W uses every pre-election week as an observation with a residual block bootstrap conditional on the forecast path; there is no event-window design around large forecast moves.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Needs dated forecast histories with run timestamps (in hand for 2022 per sgs_seats.R:93) and transaction-dated giving; works only if specific forecast jumps come from news plausibly unrelated to donor behaviour (a court ruling, a model update) and giving is observed finely enough around them. Any such result stays UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it (DE-062) and must name its window and denominator.

bearings.paper_claim: Partisan shock coded as the Republican-win indicator minus the pre-election market probability (a surprise); over 1880-2004 it gives about 0.025 (SE about 0.008) on equities, while an incumbent-party term adds nothing (-0.0046, SE 0.0084). Congressional control could not be tested because markets did not track it before 1994.
bearings.paper_location: Historical evidence section, Table 3 p.17, Figure 4 p.16, fn 19 p.17
bearings.system_side: The SHIFT regression puts Shift = P - RMajNow (expected minus current chamber control) on the right of RShare, built as exp_shift = expected Democratic control minus current. Preview: chamber-stacked -0.04, p .76 (2021-25), no stable partisan shift; year fixed effects cannot identify national P or Shift.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Shift measures an expected change in control before the election; the paper's shock is realized outcome minus prior expectation, which applies only to post-election giving (the cycle after an upset). Transfers if Mentat holds as-of pre-election control probabilities per chamber per cycle; the number of independent shocks equals the number of elections, so any estimate is few-cluster and must say so.

gaps_exposed: SEATS-W states no identifying assumption about common shocks between forecasts and giving; the as-of lag handles ordering only. The -3.47 pp per seat slope (2022 House, 17 weeks, one election) is a correlation until an exogenous-jump design or a second cycle reproduces it.
The sector growth study has no event-window or surprise-coded design; 538 run timestamps for 2022 would allow one.
SHIFT and SEATS use expected control or seats but never the post-election surprise (realized minus expected), the quantity with the cleanest identification in this literature.
The plan cites the QJE 2007 version; the file on disk is the IZA 2006 working paper, and numbers may differ between versions.
flags: Any reading of the SEATS-W negative slope as donors moving toward or away from the expected winner would conflict with this paper's evidence that campaign-period time-series slopes can be inflated about tenfold or sign-reversed; keep it EXPLORATORY and quote it with its window (2022 House, 17 weeks) and denominator.
Version mismatch: the plan and missing_sources.md cite Snowberg, Wolfers and Zitzewitz 2007 QJE 122(2); this file is the 2006 IZA DP 1996 draft. Cite numbers as the 2006 draft.
No conflict with the SNA, LDA (D-021), D-025 or reciprocity rules: the paper concerns asset prices, not networks, edges or lobbying weights.
paul_alignment: Paul has no annotated entry and no markup for this work. His sector growth plan cites the 2007 published version as background on seat-gain and control effects (it was listed as a missing source). The evidence supports using forecast probabilities as the predictor, as SEATS and SHIFT already do, but cuts against a causal reading of the weekly slope: the paper's core point is that campaign-period regressions mix effect and feedback. The current build answers his seat-gain question descriptively, matching the EXPLORATORY label in sgs_seats.R; nothing in his notes is stale.

related.why: Furnas prices a change in House control for party-tied lobbying firms; Snowberg prices a change in presidential party for asset markets. Both value partisan control shocks, the question SEATS and SHIFT ask of giving.
Imai and Kim warn about causal claims from two-way fixed-effects panels; Snowberg warns about campaign-period time-series slopes. Together they bound what the SHIFT and SEATS-W regressions can claim.
